narrative: The model estimated a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, so your law school application was denied because the forecast crossed the school’s risk threshold. This is not a final judgment about your ability; it is a warning signal based on the academic profile most associated with bar failure. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile, and that standing pushed the prediction toward failure more than anything else. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor; at 19 versus an accepted-student average of about 37, it also pushed toward failure. Your first-year class standing was third; at the first decile versus an accepted average near the sixth, it added further risk. All three top factors pointed in the same direction—toward likely bar failure—which explains why the denial was firm despite other details such as middle family income and part-time status. To improve a future application, focus on the signals you can change: build a stronger academic record, prepare for and retake the LSAT, and seek advising on bar-exam readiness and study supports. Reapplication after demonstrated improvement would give the model a materially different profile to assess.
